title: The Moon's orbit and its phases
keyIdea: The Moon is a ball of rock that makes no light of its own. It shines because sunlight bounces off it. The Sun always lights half of the Moon, the half facing the Sun. The Moon travels round Earth, and it takes about 29 and a half days to go from one new moon to the next. As it goes round, we see different amounts of its sunlit half. At new moon it is between Earth and the Sun, so the lit half faces away and we see nothing. At full moon it is on the far side of Earth, so the whole lit half faces us. Earth's shadow does not make the phases.
familyTip: In a dark room, shine a lamp from one side and hold a ball at arm's length. Turn slowly on the spot and watch the ball: it goes from dark to a crescent, a half, nearly full and full, then back. The ball is always half lit by the lamp; your head is Earth. Then check the real Moon for a week and draw its shape each evening.

visual.caption: Which give out their own light, and which only shine when light bounces off them? Drag each one into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: switch the Sun off, move the Moon round Earth, see its shape from Earth, test the shadow idea and order a month of shapes.

kid: The Moon is a big ball of rock. It makes no light. It shines because light from the Sun bounces off it. If the Sun went out, the Moon would go dark.
The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. That is the half that faces the Sun. The other half is dark, like night on Earth.
The Moon goes round and round Earth. Its path is called an orbit. One trip, from new moon to new moon, takes about 29 and a half days. That is about a month.

As the Moon goes round, we see more or less of its bright half. At new moon the bright half faces away from us. At full moon it all faces us. The shape we see is called a phase. Earth's shadow does not make it.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This builds on observing Moon shapes and explains their cause, as in NGSS 5-ESS1-2 (patterns in the sky) and the middle-school standard MS-ESS1-1 (lunar phases explained by the Earth, Sun and Moon system), and the Year 5 'Earth and space' unit in England (the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth). Key words: orbit, reflect, sunlit half, phase, new moon, crescent, first quarter, gibbous, full moon, last quarter.

The Moon is always half lit by the Sun. Its phase is how much of that sunlit half faces Earth. Seen from above the North Pole, the Moon goes anticlockwise. From new moon to new moon takes about 29.5 days (the synodic month); one orbit against the stars takes about 27.3 days, but the phase cycle is longer because Earth moves along its own orbit meanwhile. In the Northern Hemisphere a growing (waxing) Moon is lit on the right; in the Southern Hemisphere it looks the other way round.

Common mistakes: thinking the Moon makes its own light; thinking Earth's shadow causes the phases (that is a lunar eclipse, which can only happen at full moon); thinking only the part we see is lit; putting the full moon between Earth and the Sun; and expecting the cycle to take a night or a year.

In the lab your child switches the Sun off and sees the Moon go dark, moves the Moon once round Earth and counts the days, drags it round while a window shows its shape from Earth, taps eight Moons that are all half lit, finds the one place Earth's shadow could reach, and puts seven Moon shapes in order.

practice.prompt: Why can we see the Moon at night?
practice.hint: Think about what happened in the lab when the Sun was switched off.
practice.explain: The Moon makes no light. Sunlight bounces off it, so we see the half the Sun lights.

practice.prompt: There is a new moon on day {a} of the month. A half moon comes about 7 days later. On about which day is the half moon?
practice.hint: Add the 7 days to the day of the new moon.
practice.explain: Day {a} + 7 days = about day {=a+7}. A quarter of the way round Earth takes about a week.

practice.prompt: There is a full moon on day {a}. It takes about 15 days to go from full moon to new moon. On about which day is the next new moon?
practice.hint: Full moon to new moon is half of the trip round Earth.
practice.explain: Day {a} + 15 = about day {=a+15}. Half of the 29 and a half day cycle is about 15 days.

practice.prompt: Where is the Moon when we see a full moon?
choices: On the far side of Earth from the Sun
practice.hint: At full moon, the whole sunlit half faces us.
practice.explain: At full moon the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, so its sunlit half faces Earth. It usually passes just above or below Earth's shadow.

practice.prompt: We see a thin crescent Moon. How much of the Moon is the Sun lighting?
practice.hint: The Sun lights one half of the Moon all the time.
practice.explain: Half the Moon is always lit. At a crescent, most of that lit half faces away from Earth, so we see a thin curve.

choices: Its path round the Sun only
The way it spins on the spot
pool.hint: In the lab you moved the Moon along a circle.
pool.explain: The Moon's orbit is its path round Earth. One trip from new moon to new moon takes about 29 and a half days.

pool.prompt: What causes the phases of the Moon?
choices: Seeing more or less of its sunlit half
pool.hint: Every Moon in the lab was half lit.
pool.explain: The phase is how much of the sunlit half faces Earth. Earth's shadow is not part of it.

pool.prompt: At new moon, where is the Moon?
choices: On the far side of Earth
pool.hint: At new moon the lit half faces away from us.
pool.explain: At new moon the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, so its sunlit half faces away and we see it dark.

pool.prompt: About how long is it from one new moon to the next?
pool.hint: In the lab you counted the days for one trip round Earth.
pool.explain: About 29 and a half days, roughly a month. The word month comes from Moon.

pool.prompt: There is a half moon (first quarter) on day {a}. Full moon comes about 7 days later. On about which day is the full moon?
pool.hint: Half moon to full moon is another quarter of the trip, about a week.
pool.explain: Day {a} + 7 = about day {=a+7}. Each quarter of the trip round Earth takes about a week.

pool.prompt: In the north of the world, a Moon is lit on the right and growing. What will it look like in a few days?
pool.hint: Growing Moons get more lit each night until full moon.
pool.explain: A Moon lit on the right is growing (waxing), so it gets fuller each night until full moon.

pool.prompt: If the Sun could switch off, what would happen to the Moon?
pool.hint: Does the Moon make light, or bounce it?
pool.explain: The Moon only reflects sunlight, so with no Sun it would go dark.

pool.prompt: The Moon goes a quarter of the way round Earth in about 7 days. About how many days does it take to go {a} quarters of the way round?
pool.hint: Each quarter of the trip takes about a week, so multiply by 7.
pool.explain: {a} × 7 = about {=7*a} days. A whole trip is really a little more than 4 weeks, about 29 and a half days.

pool.prompt: Does the Moon really change shape during the month?
choices: No, it is always a round ball
pool.hint: Think about the eight Moons in the lab.
pool.explain: The Moon is always round. Only the part of its lit half that faces us changes.
